How to Use This Book

This book answers every Section A question set in the last three MTE 4107 examinations (term examinations held in 2022, 2023 and 2024, i.e. the 2018, 2019 and 2020 batches). It is arranged by topic, not by year: each chapter first teaches the theory from the beginning, then solves the past questions on that topic. Each question is quoted exactly as printed on the paper, with its year, number and marks. No question was repeated word for word between the three papers, so each of the 36 question parts is answered separately.

■ Theory box
Definitions and results to write in the exam.
■ Formula box
Equations to memorise; all are collected in the Appendix.
■ Exam box
How to lay out the answer and what earns marks.
■ Caution box
Common mistakes, misprints in the papers and the assumptions used.
■ Insight box
Intuition and engineering meaning.

1. Mechatronic Systems and the Design Process ★★★

1.1 What Mechatronics Is

The word mechatronics was coined by the Yaskawa Electric Company: "mecha" from mechanism and "tronics" from electronics. Yaskawa's idea was that products would incorporate electronics into mechanisms so intimately and organically that it becomes impossible to tell where one ends and the other begins.

Definition (Harashima, Tomizuka and Fukuda, 1996)
Mechatronics is the synergistic integration of mechanical engineering with electronics and intelligent computer control in the design and manufacture of industrial products and processes.
Synergy means that the combined system is more capable than the sum of its separately designed parts: a cheap sensor plus clever software can replace a precisely machined (expensive) mechanism, a flexible arm plus feedback can behave like a stiff one, and so on.

Evolution. Automatic control is old (Greek float regulators, 300–1 B.C.), and "automation" was popularised by Ford in the 1940s for transfer machines. The four industrial revolutions show the trend: (1) late 1700s–mid 1800s, purely mechanical machines; (2) late 1800s–early 1900s, electricity and mass production; (3) late 1900s, electronics, computers and automation; (4) 2000s–present, smart, connected systems with AI. Falling prices of electronics (a high performance-to-cost ratio) and the demand for very small systems pushed mechanical products steadily towards mechatronic ones.

1.2 Key Elements of a Mechatronic System

Every mechatronic system is built from the same building blocks. The mechanical system does the physical work; actuators drive it; sensors measure what it is doing; a controller (hardware plus software) compares the measurement with the desired value and decides the next actuator command.

ElementWhat it does and what to consider when choosing itExamples
Mechanical componentsStructures, frames, gears, linkages, springs, bearings. They give physical movement and structural support. Design attention: price, shape, weight, size, and the operating environment, which decides the material (iron, aluminium, plastic, composite …).Robot arm links and joints, gripper, gearbox, frame of a CNC machine
SensorsMeasure physical variables (position, speed, force, temperature …) and convert them to electrical signals. Selection criteria: error/precision/resolution, range (span), nonlinearity, repeatability, hysteresis, stability/drift, reliability, cost, ease of use.Encoder, accelerometer, gyroscope, camera, proximity sensor, strain gauge
ActuatorsProduce motion or force from a control signal. Selection criteria: power-to-weight ratio, operating environment, required stiffness. In a mine (sparks may cause fire) electric actuators are excluded and hydraulics are used; in the food industry hydraulics are excluded (oil contamination) and electric or pneumatic actuators are used.DC/servo/stepper motor, hydraulic cylinder, pneumatic piston, solenoid
Control systemThe algorithm and logic that process sensor data and decide actuator commands; open-loop or closed-loop (feedback).PID position loop of a motor
Microcontroller / embedded systemThe "brain": reads the inputs, runs the control algorithm, sends commands; includes the interface (ADC, DAC, PWM, communication).Arduino, PLC, DSP or dedicated embedded processor
Three solution domains
Mechanical design is mainly concerned with spatial relationships and interactions; electronic design with signal processing and the interconnection of components; software design with data and information-processing algorithms. A mechatronic designer must trade functions between the three domains.

1.3 Classical (Sequential) and Mechatronic (Concurrent) Design Approaches

In the classical design approach the mechanical design is done first. Once a satisfactory mechanical design exists, the electronic system is designed, and in the final stage the control system is designed. In the mechatronic design approach the mechanical, electronic and control systems are designed together, taking into account how the design of each affects the other two. The mechanical system is finalised only after studying the effect of that design on the electronics and on the control system.

Why the mechatronic approach is better. In the classical approach the mechanical design, once fixed, is final: its materials and size dictate (and limit) the choice of motors and their positions, which in turn limits the choice of instrumentation and control. In the mechatronic approach each subsystem can be chosen so that the overall performance is best. For example, a lighter and more flexible arm can be accepted if the controller damps its vibration.

Concurrent engineering. The Institute for Defense Analysis (Report R-338) defines it as "a systematic approach to the integrated, concurrent design of products and their related processes, including manufacture and support", which makes developers consider every life-cycle element from concept through disposal (quality, cost, schedule and user requirements) from the outset. Interdisciplinary teams make trade-offs about manufacturability, testability and serviceability in real time; the aim is "right first time" instead of "redo until right". The conceptual phase may be longer, but removing late design iterations reduces total development cost and time to market.

Why it was needed. Mass production after the industrial revolution split design and manufacturing into separate specialist departments. "Walls" grew between them and reinforced the sequential process: each department threw its result "over the wall" to the next, the development cycle lengthened and companies lost competitiveness. New products earn most of their revenue early in their life, and defects found after release cause recalls and lost customer loyalty.

Conventional designMechatronic design
Added components → integration of components (hardware)
BulkyCompact
Complex mechanismsSimple mechanisms
Cable problemsBus or wireless communication
Connected componentsAutonomous units
Simple control → integration by information processing (software)
Stiff constructionElastic construction with damping by electronic feedback
Feedforward, linear (analog) controlProgrammable feedback (nonlinear), digital control
Precision through narrow tolerancesPrecision through measurement and feedback control
Non-measurable quantities change arbitrarilyControl of non-measurable, estimated quantities
Simple monitoringSupervision with fault diagnosis
Fixed abilitiesLearning abilities

1.4 Design-Process Models (Design and Development Process / Life-Cycle Design)

The lecture shows four models of the design and development process (DDP), after Bradley et al.

  • Sequential (waterfall) model: requirement analysis and specification → architectural design → detailed design → manufacture → test → deploy → maintain. Each phase starts when the previous one ends; errors found late are expensive.
  • V-model (adapted from NASA): the left leg decomposes and defines (user requirements → system requirements → architectural design → detailed design); the bottom is assembly and integration; the right leg integrates and verifies, each test level being "checked by" the matching design level (unit tests ↔ detailed design, integration tests ↔ architecture, system tests ↔ system requirements, acceptance tests ↔ user requirements).
  • Prototyping model: requirements gathering → quick design → build prototype → customer evaluation → refine requirements (loop) until the customer accepts; then design → implement → test → maintain.
  • Concurrent model: after requirements definition, market requirements, design for manufacture, conceptual design, design for testability and quality mechanisms proceed together, feeding design embodiment, service and support systems and manufacturing processes, then manufacture and product.

1.5 Recognition of Need

Definition
Recognition of need is the very first step of the design process: identifying and clearly defining a problem or opportunity that requires a solution, i.e. answering "What exactly are we trying to achieve, and why?". It is "finding the why before working on the how".
  • The need may come from market demand, safety requirements, efficiency improvements or new technology possibilities.
  • The need must be real, specific and justified, not a vague wish.
  • It sets the direction for every later stage; it is refined into the design specification (speed, accuracy, cost limits …).
  • Without it the team risks designing a good solution to the wrong problem.
Source of needPractical example (lecture)
Market demandElectric vehicles: consumers wanted environmentally friendly transport and lower fuel costs.
Safety requirementAirbags and ABS brakes: seat belts alone were not enough to protect passengers.
Efficiency improvementIncandescent bulbs replaced by LED lighting for higher efficiency and longer life.
New technologyTouch-screen technology led to smartphones and tablets, creating new markets.

1.6 Phases of Product Design and Integrated Design Issues

Most engineering design texts (Pahl and Beitz; Bradley et al.) divide the work after the need has been recognised into four main phases:

  1. Clarification of the task (product planning and specification). Collect information about the requirements and constraints and write the requirements list (specification): demands (must be met) and wishes (desirable).
  2. Conceptual design. Abstract the problem, set up the function structure (overall function split into sub-functions), search for working principles for each sub-function, combine them into concept variants, and evaluate them against technical and economic criteria to pick the best concept.
  3. Embodiment design. Turn the concept into a definitive layout: arrangement, preliminary sizes, materials, choice of standard parts (motors, bearings, gears), strength, stiffness and safety checks, cost estimate.
  4. Detail design. Final form, dimensions, tolerances and surface finish of every part; drawings, bill of materials, software code, assembly, test and production documents.

These are followed by prototype manufacture and testing, production, launch and service. Iteration back to an earlier phase happens whenever a later phase shows that an earlier decision does not work.

Integrated design issues in mechatronics
Challenges: multidisciplinary modelling; simultaneous consideration of designs from different disciplines (cross-functional teams); lack of tools and methods that support multidisciplinary design.
Solutions: a single system model, used and changed by engineers of all disciplines, written in a visually intuitive environment (block diagrams, flow charts, state-transition diagrams, bond graphs) such as Simulink, LabVIEW or MATRIXx, which can also generate C code for the target; and integration of mechanical and electrical CAD by bidirectional propagation of cross-disciplinary constraints.

1.7 Past Question: The Four Questions in Mechatronic System Design

2022 · Q1(a)What are the four questions that should be considered when designing a mechatronics system? 08Topic: design questions for a mechatronic system

Before choosing hardware, a designer answers four questions. Each one fixes a major part of the design.

  1. Is system dynamics important? If the speed of response matters for stability and for the time-response specification (overshoot, rise time, settling time), the dynamics must be modelled and the controller designed from a dynamic model of the whole loop (plant, actuator, sensor, controller). Dynamics usually matter when (i) the system must respond quickly to a change of reference or to disturbances, and/or (ii) an accurate, exact value of the controlled variable is needed. Examples: a quad-rotor, an inverted pendulum and an active vehicle suspension (dynamics critical); a slowly heated room or an iris scanner (a static or simple model is enough).
  2. What type of component should be selected for each of the four main elements? Choose the sensors (type, range, resolution, bandwidth), the actuators (electric, hydraulic, pneumatic; power-to-weight, environment, stiffness), the controller (control law such as on–off, P, PI, PD, PID, and the hardware: PLC, PC, microcontroller, relays) and the mechanical components (structure, transmission, bearings, materials).
  3. Is open-loop control sufficient, or is closed-loop (feedback) control needed? If disturbances, load changes or parameter variations would make the output wrong, feedback is required, which brings in sensors, a control law and a stability analysis. Open-loop control (for example a stepper motor driven by a known pulse train) is cheaper when the process is repeatable and disturbances are small.
  4. How will the subsystems be integrated and interfaced? Decide the signal conditioning (amplification, filtering, isolation), the conversion (ADC/DAC, PWM, encoder counters), the communication (bus or wireless), the power supply, and how mechanical, electronic and software parts will be tested together (simulation, prototyping, hardware-in-the-loop) before the product is built.
Note on the source
The four questions are not in AJ's slides. Questions 1 and 2 follow the commonly used course note "Four questions to ask when designing mechatronics systems"; the wording of questions 3 and 4 differs between sources, so explain each question with an example, as above, to earn the marks.
Source lectureAJ · L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 8–11) — the four questions themselves are not in the slides — see §1.7

1.8 Past Question: Classical versus Concurrent Design Approach

2022 · Q1(b)Compare between the classical design approach and concurrent design approach with proper block diagram. 10Topic: classical vs concurrent design

Block diagrams: draw Figure 1.2. In (a) the mechanical, electronic and control/instrumentation designs follow one another with one-way arrows. In (b) the three designs are carried out together around a shared system model and requirements, with two-way arrows showing their interactions. The concurrent design model of Figure 1.3(b) can be drawn as a fuller version.

AspectClassical (sequential) approachConcurrent (mechatronic) approach
Order of workMechanical first, then electronics, then control, one after anotherMechanical, electronic, control and manufacturing designed at the same time by one team
Interaction between domainsIgnored: each stage accepts the previous stage's result as fixedConsidered from the start: each design is checked for its effect on the other two
Freedom of choiceThe mechanical design limits motor size and location, which limits sensors and controlBest combination for overall performance; functions can be moved between hardware and software
Life-cycle factorsConsidered after the product is designed and manufacturedManufacture, test, service, quality and disposal included during design
TeamsSeparate specialist departments with "walls" between themCross-functional (multidisciplinary) team, real-time trade-offs
Iterations and errors"Redo until right"; errors found late, expensive changes and recalls"Right first time"; problems caught early
Development time and costLong cycle, higher total costLonger concept phase but shorter overall time to market and lower total cost
Resulting productBulky, stiff, complex mechanisms, precision by tight tolerancesCompact, simpler mechanisms, precision by measurement and feedback
Answer in one line
Classical design optimises each domain separately and in sequence; concurrent (mechatronic) design optimises the whole system by designing all domains, and the life-cycle processes, together.
Source lectureAJ · L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 13–14); L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 18–22)

1.9 Past Question: How the Mechatronic Approach Differs

2023 · Q1(c)How mechatronic system design approach is different from earlier design approach? Briefly explain. 12Topic: mechatronic vs conventional design

Earlier (conventional, classical) approach. The mechanical system is designed first. When a satisfactory mechanical design exists, the electronic system is designed for it, and finally the control system. Each discipline works on its own and receives the previous result as fixed (Figure 1.2a).

Mechatronic approach. The mechanical, electronic and control (software) systems are designed together, considering how the design of each one affects the other two. The mechanical design is finalised only after its effect on the electronics and the control system has been studied (Figure 1.2b). The main differences are:

  1. Simultaneous instead of sequential design. All domains, and the life-cycle processes (manufacture, test, service), are considered from the start by a cross-functional team (concurrent engineering).
  2. Global instead of local optimum. In the earlier approach, once the materials and size of the mechanism are fixed they limit the motors (size, position), which limits the sensors and controller. The mechatronic approach can choose the best combination for overall performance.
  3. Functions moved into electronics and software. Precision comes from measurement and feedback instead of narrow tolerances; a light, elastic structure is damped electronically instead of being made stiff and heavy; complex mechanisms are replaced by simple ones plus programmable motion.
  4. Integration of hardware. Bulky, cable-heavy, separately connected components become compact autonomous units linked by a bus or wireless network.
  5. Integration by information processing. Simple analog feedforward control and simple monitoring become programmable digital (nonlinear) control, estimation of non-measurable quantities, supervision with fault diagnosis and even learning abilities.
  6. Model-based, simulation-heavy design. Models, simulation and hardware-in-the-loop testing are used to check the integrated design before building it, and prototyping absorbs the unmodelled errors.
  7. Business result. "Right first time": fewer late iterations, lower development cost, shorter time to market and fewer recalls.

The comparison table of §1.3 (conventional vs mechatronic design) summarises points 3–5 and should be reproduced in the answer.

Source lectureAJ · L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 13–14); L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 20–23)

1.10 Past Question: Key Elements With Examples

2023 · Q1(b)What are the key elements of a mechatronic system? Give example of each of the elements. 08Topic: key elements of a mechatronic system

The key elements are the main building blocks that work together to make the system function (Figure 1.1):

  1. Mechanical components: structures, frames, gears, linkages, springs, bearings; they give the physical movement and support. Example: robot arm joints and grippers.
  2. Sensors: measure physical variables (temperature, position, speed, force) and convert them into electrical signals. Examples: encoders, accelerometers, gyroscopes, cameras (image sensors), proximity sensors.
  3. Actuators: produce motion or force from control signals. Examples: electric motors, hydraulic cylinders, pneumatic pistons.
  4. Control system: the algorithms and logic that process the sensor data and decide the actuator commands, open- or closed-loop. Example: PID controller of a motor.
  5. Microcontroller / embedded system: the "brain" that reads inputs, runs the control algorithm and sends commands. Examples: Arduino, PLC, dedicated embedded processor.

(Signal conditioning and interfacing, i.e. amplifiers, ADC/DAC and drivers, connect the sensors and actuators to the controller.)

Source lectureAJ · L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 8–11)

1.11 Past Question: Key Elements Applied to a Robotic Manipulator

2024 · Q1(a)What are the key elements of mechatronic systems? How do they apply to a robotic manipulator? 06Topic: key elements — robot manipulator

The key elements are mechanical components, sensors, actuators, the control system and the microcontroller/embedded computer (§1.2). In an industrial robotic manipulator:

ElementIn a robotic manipulator
Mechanical systemBase, links, revolute/prismatic joints, harmonic-drive or planetary gearboxes, belts, bearings, wrist and gripper (end effector)
ActuatorsA brushless servo motor (with brake) at each joint; pneumatic or electric gripper actuator
SensorsJoint encoders/resolvers (position, speed), motor current sensors (torque), wrist force/torque sensor, camera for vision guidance, limit and proximity switches for safety
Control systemInverse kinematics and trajectory planning; a PID (or computed-torque) position loop per joint; safety interlocks
Microcontroller / embedded systemRobot controller cabinet (embedded processors, servo drives, I/O), teach pendant, communication with the cell PLC

Together they form the loop of Figure 1.1: the controller computes the joint commands, the drives and motors move the links through the gears, the encoders feed the actual joint angles back, and the controller corrects the error so the end effector follows the desired path.

1.12 Past Question: Recognition of Need and Its Importance

2023 · Q1(a)What is recognition of need? Why is it important in design? 05Topic: recognition of need

Recognition of need is the first step of the design process: identifying and clearly defining the problem or opportunity that needs a solution, answering "What exactly are we trying to achieve, and why?". It may come from market demand, safety requirements, efficiency improvements or new technology. Example: "We need a device that automatically sorts packages by size to speed up warehouse processing."

Why it is important:

  1. It sets the direction of every later stage: the need is refined into the design specification (speed, accuracy, cost limits), the concepts and the tests.
  2. It ensures the need is real, specific and justified, not a vague wish, so resources are spent on a worthwhile product.
  3. It prevents designing a good solution to the wrong problem, which wastes time and money and leads to products the market does not want.
  4. It gives the criteria against which concepts are evaluated and the final product is accepted.
Source lectureAJ · L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 24–25)

1.13 Past Question: Recognition of Need With a Practical Example

2024 · Q1(b)What is recognition of need? Give practical example of it. 05Topic: recognition of need — example

Recognition of need is the very first step of design: identifying and clearly defining a problem or opportunity that requires a solution ("What are we trying to achieve, and why?"). The need must be real, specific and justified, and it is later refined into the design specification. In short, it finds the "why" before the "how".

Practical examples (one per source of need):

  • Safety requirement: it was recognised that seat belts alone did not protect passengers well enough in crashes and that locked wheels make a car unsteerable; this need led to airbags and ABS brakes.
  • Market demand: customers wanted environmentally friendly transport and lower fuel costs, which led to electric vehicles.
  • Efficiency improvement: the need for higher energy efficiency and longer lamp life led from incandescent bulbs to LED lighting.
  • New technology: touch-screen technology created smartphones and tablets.
  • Industrial example: "We need a device to automatically sort packages by size to speed up warehouse processing", later refined into a specification (throughput, sorting accuracy, cost limit).
Source lectureAJ · L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 24–25)

1.14 Past Question: Design Phases of a Pallet Transporter

2024 · Q2(b)Following some initial market assessments the board of a plant machinery company has decided to proceed with the design of a new product for transporting pallets around factories. Briefly explain the phases in design to develop this product. 15Topic: phases of the design process

The need has already been recognised (the board's decision after market assessment). The product, for example an automated guided vehicle (AGV) or powered pallet truck, is then developed through the phases of Figure 1.4. Iteration back to an earlier phase happens whenever a later phase shows a problem.

Phase 1 — Clarification of the task (specification). Collect the requirements from the market study, customers, standards and the company, and write the requirements list with demands and wishes. For the pallet transporter: pallet size and maximum load (e.g. 1000–1500 kg on a Euro pallet), lift height, travel speed and acceleration, routes and floor conditions, aisle width and turning radius, operating time per battery charge, navigation (manual, line-following or laser-guided), positioning accuracy at pick-up and drop-off, safety (obstacle detection, emergency stop, speed limits near people, relevant machine-safety standards), interfaces to the factory system, target cost, service life and maintenance.

Phase 2 — Conceptual design. State the overall function ("move a loaded pallet safely from A to B") and split it into sub-functions: lift and hold the pallet, propel, steer, brake, store energy, sense position and obstacles, plan the path, communicate, interact with the operator. For each, search for working principles (e.g. lift: hydraulic or electric screw; drive: differential drive or steered drive wheel; navigation: magnetic tape, laser reflectors or vision/SLAM; energy: lead-acid or lithium battery). Combine them into concept variants with a morphological chart, then evaluate (cost, safety, flexibility, technical risk) and select the best concept.

Phase 3 — Embodiment design. Develop the chosen concept into a definitive layout: chassis and fork geometry, centre of gravity and stability, load cases and strength/stiffness of the frame, wheel and bearing selection, motor and gearbox sizing from the speed and acceleration profile, battery capacity, lifting mechanism, sensor placement, controller and drive electronics architecture, software structure, preliminary cost and safety (risk) analysis. Here the mechatronic (concurrent) approach is applied: mechanics, electronics and control are sized together.

Phase 4 — Detail design. Final dimensions, tolerances, materials and surface finish of every part; detailed drawings and bill of materials; wiring diagrams and PCB design; control and navigation software code; assembly, test and production documents.

Then: prototype, test and launch. Build a prototype; test it (simulation and hardware-in-the-loop for the controller, then load, endurance, braking, obstacle-detection and safety tests); correct the design; plan production; launch; provide service and support; feed field experience back into the next version.

What earns marks
Name the four phases in order (clarification of task → conceptual → embodiment → detail), say what each phase produces (specification, concept, layout, documents), apply each to the pallet transporter, and mention iteration and the concurrent (mechatronic) approach.
Source lectureAJ · L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 15–18) — named design phases (clarification, conceptual, embodiment, detail) not in slides — see §1.6

2. System Modelling and Linearization ★★★

2.1 Modelling: What It Is and How Models Are Obtained

Definition
Modelling is the process of representing the behaviour of a real system by a collection of mathematical equations and logic. A model is a cause-and-effect structure: it accepts external information (inputs, parameters), processes it with its equations and logic, and produces one or more outputs (signals, usually functions of time).
  • Static models involve no energy transfer and therefore no motion or change (e.g. a gain, a spring under a constant load). Dynamic models include energy transfer and power flow, which cause motion, heat transfer, fluid flow and other changes in time; they are differential (or difference) equations.
  • Static and dynamic process models are needed for simulation, control design and variable reconstruction (estimating quantities that cannot be measured).
  • Modular structure. A model should be built from blocks. A first-principles block captures the fundamental behaviour of a subsystem; a detailed block extends it with more functions and accuracy. Each block has inputs limited to input signals and parameters and outputs limited to output signals, so blocks can be tested on their own, swapped (first-principles ↔ detailed), reused and reconfigured.
  • Unmodelled errors. No model reproduces reality exactly; the difference (unmodelled dynamics) is why many model-based designs fail when deployed. The mechatronic approach absorbs these errors in the prototyping step. Example: early smartphones whose thermal models underestimated worst-case processor heat overheated, and some batteries caught fire; later designs added better thermal models, heat pipes and software thermal throttling.
Two ways to obtain a mathematical model
1. Theoretical (physical, first-principles, "white-box") modelling — write the physical laws of each component (Newton's laws, Kirchhoff's laws, conservation of mass and energy, constitutive laws such as F=kxF=kxF=kx, v=Riv=Riv=Ri) and combine them. Parameters have physical meaning. The principles for systems with energy flow are the same across the electrical, mechanical and thermal domains; material flows (fluidics, thermodynamics, chemical processes) make it harder.
2. Experimental modelling (system identification, "black-box") — apply known inputs u(k)u(k)u(k) to the real system, record the outputs y(k)y(k)y(k), choose a model structure (e.g. first order plus dead time, ARX, transfer function of order nnn) and fit its parameters so the model matches the data.
Combined (grey-box): the structure comes from physics, unknown parameter values from experiments (e.g. motor KtK_tKt​, JJJ, DDD fitted from a step test).
AspectTheoretical modellingExperimental identification
NeedsKnowledge of the physics and parameter valuesA working system (or prototype) and measurements
ValidityWide range, also before the hardware existsOnly near the tested operating conditions
ParametersPhysical meaning (mass, resistance …)Often no physical meaning
EffortHigh for complex processesFast for complex processes; needs good test signals and data

2.5 Linearization

Definition
Linearization is the replacement of a nonlinear model x˙=f(x,u)\dot{\mathbf x}=\mathbf f(\mathbf x,\mathbf u)x˙=f(x,u) by a linear model that is valid for small deviations about an operating (equilibrium) point (x0,u0)(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf u_0)(x0​,u0​), obtained by keeping only the first-order (linear) terms of the Taylor series.

Procedure.

  1. Write the nonlinear state equations x˙i=fi(x,u)\dot x_i=f_i(\mathbf x,\mathbf u)x˙i​=fi​(x,u).
  2. Find the equilibrium: set all derivatives to zero, f(x0,u0)=0\mathbf f(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf u_0)=\mathbf 0f(x0​,u0​)=0.
  3. Define small deviations δx=x−x0\delta\mathbf x=\mathbf x-\mathbf x_0δx=x−x0​, δu=u−u0\delta\mathbf u=\mathbf u-\mathbf u_0δu=u−u0​.
  4. Expand in a Taylor series and keep the first-order terms: f(x0+δx)≈f(x0)+∂f∂x∣0δx.f(x_0+\delta x)\approx f(x_0)+\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Big|_{0}\delta x.f(x0​+δx)≈f(x0​)+∂x∂f​​0​δx.
  5. Write the linear state-space model δx˙=A δx+B δu\delta\dot{\mathbf x}=\mathbf A\,\delta\mathbf x+\mathbf B\,\delta\mathbf uδx˙=Aδx+Bδu,  δy=C δx\ \delta\mathbf y=\mathbf C\,\delta\mathbf x δy=Cδx, with the Jacobians Aij=∂fi∂xj∣0,Bij=∂fi∂uj∣0.A_{ij}=\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\Big|_0,\qquad B_{ij}=\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial u_j}\Big|_0.Aij​=∂xj​∂fi​​​0​,Bij​=∂uj​∂fi​​​0​.

2.6 Past Question: Modelling of a Process and the Ways to Obtain a Model

2022 · Q3(a)What is modeling of a process? What are the ways to obtain a mathematical model of a process? Briefly explain them. 12Topic: modelling — theoretical and experimental

Modelling of a process is the process of representing the behaviour of a real system (process) by a collection of mathematical equations and logic. The model is a cause-and-effect structure that takes inputs and parameters and produces outputs that reproduce the behaviour of the real process. Models are static (no energy transfer, no change with time) or dynamic (energy transfer and power flow, so the variables change with time and the model is a set of differential equations). Static and dynamic models are needed for simulation, control design and the reconstruction of unmeasured variables.

There are two ways to obtain a mathematical model:

1. Theoretical modelling (from first, physical principles). The model is derived from the physical laws:

  • balance equations: conservation of mass, energy and momentum (Newton's second law, Kirchhoff's laws);
  • constitutive equations of each element: v=Riv=Riv=Ri, v=L di/dtv=L\,di/dtv=Ldi/dt, F=kxF=kxF=kx, F=bx˙F=b\dot xF=bx˙, T=KtiT=K_tiT=Kt​i;
  • phenomenological equations (heat transfer, friction) and the interconnection of components.

The equations are simplified (e.g. neglect small inductance or saturation) and combined into a differential equation, transfer function or state-space model. The method is unified across electrical, mechanical and thermal systems with energy flow and gets more involved with material flows. It works before the hardware exists, and its parameters have physical meaning. Example: DC motor model from KVL and Newton's law (§2.10).

2. Experimental modelling (system identification). The system is treated as a black box. Known input signals u(k)u(k)u(k) (step, pulse, PRBS, sine sweep) are applied to the real system and NNN samples of the output y(k)y(k)y(k) are recorded. Then (i) a model structure that can fit the data is chosen (e.g. first order, first order plus dead time, ARX), and (ii) its parameters are estimated (graphically, or by least squares) so the model matches the real system closely enough. The model is valid near the tested operating conditions. Example: the transfer function obtained from a step response in §2.11.

Combination (grey-box modelling): the model structure comes from theory and unknown parameters are identified from experiments. All models must finally be validated against measurements, and unmodelled errors are absorbed in the prototyping step.

Source lectureAJ · L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 30–31); L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 39–40)

2.7 Past Question: Modelling in System Design

2023 · Q2(c)What is modeling in system design? How can we get a mathematical model of a system? 05Topic: modelling

Modelling in system design means representing the behaviour of the system to be designed by mathematical equations and logic, so that it can be analysed, simulated and controlled before (and while) the hardware is built. In mechatronic design the model is built in modules (first-principles blocks that can be replaced by detailed blocks) and is shared by the mechanical, electronic and control engineers.

A mathematical model can be obtained in two ways:

  1. Theoretical (first-principles) modelling: apply the physical laws (Newton, Kirchhoff, conservation of mass and energy) and the constitutive laws of each component, then combine them into differential equations, a transfer function or a state-space model.
  2. Experimental modelling (system identification): excite the real system with known inputs, measure the outputs, choose a model structure and estimate its parameters from the measured data.

The two are often combined: the structure from physics, the parameter values from experiments.

Source lectureAJ · L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 26–31); L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, p. 39)

2.11 Past Question: What Linearization Is and Why It Matters

2022 · Q2(b)What is linearization? Why is it important? 05Topic: linearization

Linearization is the process of approximating a nonlinear system model by a linear model that is valid for small deviations about an operating (equilibrium) point. The nonlinear functions are expanded in a Taylor series about the operating point and only the first-order terms are kept: f(x)≈f(x0)+f′(x0)(x−x0)f(x)\approx f(x_0)+f'(x_0)(x-x_0)f(x)≈f(x0​)+f′(x0​)(x−x0​); for several variables the Jacobian matrices give δx˙=A δx+B δu\delta\dot{\mathbf x}=\mathbf A\,\delta\mathbf x+\mathbf B\,\delta\mathbf uδx˙=Aδx+Bδu (Figure 2.3).

Why it is important:

  1. Almost all real systems are nonlinear (magnetic force ∝i2/y\propto i^2/y∝i2/y, pendulum torque ∝sin⁡θ\propto\sin\theta∝sinθ, friction, saturation), but the powerful analysis and design tools (Laplace transform, transfer functions, root locus, Bode plots, state-space pole placement, superposition) apply only to linear models.
  2. It gives a simple model that is accurate enough near the operating point, where a regulator keeps the system.
  3. Stability of the equilibrium can be checked from the eigenvalues of A\mathbf AA (e.g. magnetic levitation and the inverted pendulum are shown to be unstable and need feedback).
  4. It allows standard controllers (PID, lead/lag, state feedback) to be designed and tuned, and gain scheduling over several operating points.
Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §2.5 of this book)

3. Simulation, Real-Time Simulation and Hardware-in-the-Loop ★★★

3.1 Simulation and Its Classification by Speed

Simulation is the process of solving the model, usually on a digital computer, to predict how the system behaves. Real-time simulation is used more and more in mechatronic design, especially when the process, the hardware and the software are developed simultaneously to shorten the development cycle and meet short time-to-market schedules. According to the required speed of computation, simulation is divided into three classes:

ClassMeaning and characteristicsTypical use and example
Simulation without (hard) time limitationThe computation may take as long as needed. The goal is accuracy, not speed; complex models can run slower than real time. Used offline.Basic investigation of behaviour, verifying theoretical models, process design, control-system design. Example: a detailed drone model where 1 s of flight takes 10 s to compute.
Real-time simulationThe simulated component produces input and output signals with the same time-dependent values as the real, dynamically operating component. Every integration step must finish within the real sampling time.Hardware-in-the-loop, operator training, control prototyping, software-in-the-loop.
Simulation faster than real timeComputes the future states faster than the real process evolves; usually needs simpler, more abstract models and sacrifices some accuracy for speed.Model-based predictive and adaptive control, online optimization, planning and scheduling. Example: a whole day of a factory conveyor simulated in 5 minutes to find bottlenecks.

3.2 Real-Time Simulation and Its Classification

Definition
Real-time simulation means that the simulation of a component is performed so that its input and output signals show the same time-dependent values as the real, dynamically operating component. This becomes a computational problem for processes whose dynamics are fast compared with the available algorithms and computing speed.

Real time is needed because one part of the investigated system is not simulated but real, so the simulated part must keep pace with it. Depending on which of the two parts of the control loop, the process (P) and the control system (C), is real, three cases are distinguished:

CaseProcessControlName and purpose
1RealSimulated (on hardware other than the final one)Control prototyping (rapid control prototyping): test new control algorithms on the real plant using a powerful development computer.
2SimulatedSimulatedSoftware-in-the-loop (SIL): run the controller software with a process model in real time when the final hardware is not available, or as the step before HIL.
3SimulatedReal control hardwareHardware-in-the-loop (HIL): test the real control unit with its series software against a real-time process model.

3.3 Hardware-in-the-Loop Simulation

HIL simulation operates real components connected to real-time simulated components. Usually the control hardware and software are real, exactly as used for series production, while the controlled process (actuators, physical process, sensors) is partly or fully simulated. Mixtures are common: often some actuators are real while the process and sensors are simulated, because actuators and control hardware frequently form one integrated subsystem, or because actuators are hard to model precisely and simulate in real time.

Advantages of HIL simulation (lecture)
  • design and testing of control hardware and software without operating the real process ("moving the process field into the laboratory");
  • testing under extreme environmental conditions in the laboratory (high/low temperature, high accelerations and shocks, aggressive media, electromagnetic compatibility);
  • testing the effects of faults and failures of actuators, sensors and computers on the overall system;
  • operating and testing extreme and dangerous operating conditions safely;
  • reproducible experiments that can be repeated frequently;
  • easy operation with different man–machine interfaces (cockpit design, operator training);
  • saving of cost and development time.

3.4 Past Question: Real-Time Simulation, Its Classes and HIL

2022 · Q1(c)What is real time simulation? Classify it. Briefly describe hardware in the loop simulation. 13Topic: real-time simulation and HIL

Real-time simulation is a simulation in which the simulated component produces input and output signals with the same time-dependent values as the real, dynamically operating component: each computation step is completed within the corresponding real time. It is required when one part of the investigated system is real, and it is computationally demanding for processes with fast dynamics. (It is one of the three classes of simulation by speed, the others being simulation without time limitation and simulation faster than real time — Figure 3.1.)

Classification (Figure 3.2), according to which part of the loop is real:

  1. Real process + simulated control → control prototyping. The control algorithm runs on a development computer (not the final hardware) connected to the real process.
  2. Simulated process + simulated control → software-in-the-loop (SIL). Both run in real time on a computer; used when the final hardware is unavailable or before HIL.
  3. Simulated process + real control system → hardware-in-the-loop (HIL).

Hardware-in-the-loop simulation. The real control unit (ECU, PLC or embedded board with its series-production software) is connected through an I/O interface to a real-time computer that simulates the process: the actuators, the physical process and the sensors (Figure 3.3). The controller sends its actuator commands to the simulator, the simulator computes the process response in real time and returns the simulated sensor signals, so the controller "believes" it is running the real machine. Often some real actuators are included and only the process and sensors are simulated.

Why HIL is used: the control hardware and software can be designed and tested without the real process (in the laboratory), under extreme environments, with injected faults of sensors, actuators and computers, in dangerous operating conditions, with reproducible and repeatable tests, with different man–machine interfaces and operator training, saving cost and development time. Example: an automotive ABS or engine ECU tested against a real-time vehicle model before road tests.

Source lectureAJ · L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 41–48)

3.5 Past Question: Software-in-the-Loop and Hardware-in-the-Loop

2023 · Q1(d)Write short note on: (i) software in loop simulation and (ii) hardware in loop simulation. 10Topic: SIL and HIL

(i) Software-in-the-loop (SIL) simulation. Both the controlled process and the control system are simulated, and they run together in real time on a computer (Figure 3.2, middle). The control software (algorithm or generated code) is executed in a loop with the process model, without the final controller hardware. It is used:

  • when the final control hardware is not yet available;
  • as the design step before HIL, to verify the control logic, timing and code generated from the block-diagram model (e.g. Simulink → C);
  • to test many scenarios cheaply and safely and find software errors early.

It does not test the real hardware, its I/O, its computation time or electrical effects.

(ii) Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation. The real control hardware with its series software is operated together with a real-time simulated process (actuators, process and sensors), connected through a real I/O interface (Figure 3.3). Frequently some actuators are real and the process and sensors are simulated. It allows testing the controller in the laboratory without the real process, under extreme environmental conditions, with injected sensor/actuator/computer faults, in dangerous conditions, with reproducible experiments, and with different man–machine interfaces, saving cost and development time.

AspectSILHIL
ControllerSimulated (software on a PC)Real hardware with series software
ProcessSimulatedSimulated in real time (some actuators may be real)
InterfaceSoftware onlyReal electrical I/O (ADC, DAC, PWM, bus)
StageEarlier: algorithm and code checksLater: hardware/software integration and validation
CostLowHigher (real-time computer and I/O)
Source lectureAJ · L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 45–48) — SIL appears only as a case in the classification — see §3.5

3.6 Past Question: Classification of Real-Time Simulation

2024 · Q1(c)Classify real-time simulation. Write short notes on each. 14Topic: real-time simulation classes

Real-time simulation means simulating a component so that its input and output signals have the same time-dependent values as the real, dynamically operating component. It is needed because one part of the system under investigation is real. With a control loop made of a process and a control system, three classes arise (Figure 3.2):

1. Control prototyping (real process, simulated control). The real process is operated together with a controller that is simulated on hardware other than the final hardware, for example a rapid-prototyping computer or a PC with I/O cards running the block-diagram controller. New control algorithms can be tried and tuned on the real plant quickly, before the final embedded controller exists. Example: trying a new suspension control law on a real test vehicle using a dSPACE-type prototyping unit.

2. Software-in-the-loop, SIL (simulated process, simulated control). The process model and the control software run together in real time. This is required when the final hardware is unavailable, or as the step before HIL, to check the control logic, timing and generated code. Example: running the generated C code of a drone autopilot against a flight model on a PC.

3. Hardware-in-the-loop, HIL (simulated process, real control system). The real control hardware and software, as used in series production, are connected to a real-time simulation of the process (actuators, process, sensors); mixtures with some real actuators are common. Advantages: testing in the laboratory without the real process, under extreme environments, with injected faults, in dangerous conditions, reproducibly, with different man–machine interfaces, saving cost and time. Example: a car engine ECU tested against a real-time engine and vehicle model.

For completeness, real-time simulation itself is one of three speed classes of simulation: without time limitation (offline, accuracy first), real time, and faster than real time (prediction, online optimization, planning) — Figure 3.1. Within the lecture's figure, real-time simulation applications are listed as process simulation (HIL, operator training), controller simulation (control prototyping) and process-plus-controller simulation.

What earns marks
Definition of real-time simulation; the three classes with "real/simulated process" and "real/simulated control" stated for each; the small C–P loop sketches of Figure 3.2; one example and the purpose of each.
Source lectureAJ · L1 – Design of Mechatronics Systems (1. Design of Mechatronics Systems_ver 1.2.pdf, pp. 42–46)

4. Mechanical System Design, Machine Elements and Ergonomics ★★★

4.1 Elements of a Mechanical System and Load Conditions

The mechanical part of a mechatronic system consists of the structure (frame, base, housings), transmission elements (shafts, gears, belts and pulleys, screws, couplings), support elements (bearings, guides, slides), connecting elements (bolts, welds, keys), springs and dampers and the end effector or tool. Each element must carry its loads without failing (strength), without deflecting too much (stiffness), for the required life (fatigue and wear), at minimum weight and cost.

Classification of loads
(a) By variation with time
• Static (steady) load: constant or applied slowly (dead weight of a machine, a preloaded bolt).
• Dynamic loads: impact/shock (suddenly applied, e.g. a hammer, a robot hitting an end stop); fluctuating/cyclic (repeated or reversed, e.g. a rotating shaft in bending, gear teeth); random (vibration from road or machine).
(b) By the deformation (stress) produced
• axial tension and compression (σ=F/A\sigma=F/Aσ=F/A), direct shear (τ=F/A\tau=F/Aτ=F/A), bending (σ=My/I\sigma=My/Iσ=My/I), torsion (τ=Tr/J\tau=Tr/Jτ=Tr/J), contact (bearing) pressure, and combined loading (e.g. a gear shaft: bending + torsion).
(c) By distribution: concentrated (point) loads, distributed loads (uniform or varying), body forces (gravity, inertia, centrifugal).
(d) By origin: dead load (self-weight), working/live load (payload, process and cutting forces, actuator forces), inertia loads from acceleration, thermal loads (constrained expansion), friction, preload, environmental loads (wind, seismic).

4.2 Machine-Design Principles

Precision-machine designers (e.g. Slocum) use a set of principles that make a structure stiff, accurate and cheap:

  • Saint-Venant's principle. The stress and strain caused by a load applied over a small region depend on how it is applied only in the neighbourhood of that region. At a distance of about one to a few times the largest dimension of the loaded area (or of the cross-section) the distribution depends only on the resultant force and moment and becomes the simple beam/bar distribution. Design rule: keep things that must not be disturbed (sensors, precision surfaces, bearing seats) several characteristic dimensions away from points of load application, clamps and bolts; and make supports and joints long enough (several dimensions) for the stress to become uniform.
  • Avoid bending stresses; use axial (tension/compression) load paths. In bending only the outer fibres are highly stressed, so material is used inefficiently and deflections are large. Loads carried axially stress the whole section uniformly and deflect far less. Design rule: triangulate structures (trusses, gussets, diagonal struts), place loads in line with supports, avoid offsets and overhangs, keep load paths short and direct.
  • Other principles: the Abbe principle (place the measurement axis in line with the working axis to avoid angle errors), exact constraint (kinematic design: constrain each degree of freedom once), symmetry (thermal and load symmetry cancels distortions), stiffness and natural frequency high enough above the control bandwidth, and minimum number of parts.

4.3 Forces on Spur Gears and Shaft Reactions

A spur-gear mesh transmits a force along the line of action, inclined at the pressure angle ϕ\phiϕ (usually 20°) to the pitch-line tangent. It is resolved into a tangential component WtW^tWt that transmits the torque and a radial component WrW^rWr that pushes the gears apart:

Gear-force relations
Wt=2Td,Wr=Wttan⁡ϕ,W=Wtcos⁡ϕ,H=WtV=Tω.W^t=\frac{2T}{d},\qquad W^r=W^t\tan\phi,\qquad W=\frac{W^t}{\cos\phi},\qquad H=W^tV=T\omega.Wt=d2T​,Wr=Wttanϕ,W=cosϕWt​,H=WtV=Tω. The radial force on a gear points towards its own centre (away from the mating gear); the tangential force on the driven gear acts in the direction of rotation at the mesh point. Shaft bearing reactions are found from equilibrium (∑F=0\sum F=0∑F=0, ∑M=0\sum M=0∑M=0) in two perpendicular planes and combined: Fr=Ry2+Rz2F_r=\sqrt{R_y^2+R_z^2}Fr​=Ry2​+Rz2​​.

4.4 Rolling-Contact Bearings: Life, Rating and Reliability

Types. Deep-groove ball bearings (radial plus moderate thrust, cheap, high speed); angular-contact ball bearings (combined radial and larger thrust); cylindrical roller bearings (heavy radial load); tapered roller bearings (heavy combined loads, used in pairs); needle bearings (small radial space); thrust bearings (axial load only). Ball bearings have point contact, roller bearings line contact and therefore a higher capacity for the same size.

Load–life relation and catalogue selection (Shigley)
Rating life L10L_{10}L10​: the number of revolutions (or hours) that 90 % of a group of identical bearings will complete before the first evidence of fatigue. The catalogue basic dynamic load rating C10C_{10}C10​ is the radial load that gives L10=106L_{10}=10^6L10​=106 revolutions (for most manufacturers, e.g. SKF).
Load–life:  F L1/a=constant\ F\,L^{1/a}=\text{constant} FL1/a=constant, with a=3a=3a=3 for ball bearings and a=10/3a=10/3a=10/3 for roller bearings.
Desired life in revolutions:  LD=60 nD LD\ L_D=60\,n_D\,\mathcal L_D LD​=60nD​LD​ (nDn_DnD​ in rev/min, LD\mathcal L_DLD​ in hours); dimensionless life xD=LD/L10x_D=L_D/L_{10}xD​=LD​/L10​.
Required rating at reliability RDR_DRD​ (three-parameter Weibull, x0=0.02x_0=0.02x0​=0.02, θ−x0=4.439\theta-x_0=4.439θ−x0​=4.439, b=1.483b=1.483b=1.483): C10=af FD[xDx0+(θ−x0)(ln⁡1RD)1/b]1/aC_{10}=a_f\,F_D\left[\frac{x_D}{x_0+(\theta-x_0)\big(\ln\frac1{R_D}\big)^{1/b}}\right]^{1/a}C10​=af​FD​​x0​+(θ−x0​)(lnRD​1​)1/bxD​​​1/a afa_faf​ = application (load) factor, 1.0 for smooth running, 1.1–1.5 for gearing with impact. If several bearings must together reach reliability RRR, each needs R1/nR^{1/n}R1/n (two bearings: R\sqrt RR​).
Combined radial and thrust load: equivalent load Fe=X V Fr+Y FaF_e=X\,V\,F_r+Y\,F_aFe​=XVFr​+YFa​ (here Fa=0F_a=0Fa​=0, so Fe=FrF_e=F_rFe​=Fr​).

Selection procedure. (1) Find the bearing reactions from the shaft loads. (2) Fix the design life LDL_DLD​ and the reliability. (3) Compute the required C10C_{10}C10​ for each bearing. 4.5 Man–Machine Interface, Industrial Design and Ergonomics

Ergonomics (human factors) designs the machine to fit the human: body dimensions (anthropometry) for reach and posture, the senses (vision, hearing, touch) for displays, and mental capacity for the tasks. The man–machine interface consists of displays (information from the machine to the person: dials, digital readouts, lamps, screens, alarms) and controls (commands from the person to the machine: switches, knobs, levers, pedals, touch-screens). Good integration of controls and displays reduces errors, reaction time, fatigue and training time. The general principles are listed in §4.9.

4.6 Past Question: Saint-Venant's Principle and Avoiding Bending Stress

2024 · Q1(d)Briefly explain the following design principles with proper example. (i) Saint Venant's principle (ii) Avoiding bending stress 10Topic: machine design principles

(i) Saint-Venant's principle. When a load is applied over a small part of a body, the local stress distribution depends on the details of how the load is applied, but at a distance of about one to a few times the largest dimension of the loaded area (or of the cross-section) the stresses depend only on the resultant force and moment; statically equivalent loads produce the same stress field far away. In Figure 4.1(a) a concentrated force on the end of a bar produces a stress peak near the end, but about one width away the stress is uniform, σ=P/A\sigma=P/Aσ=P/A.

Use in design:

  • Place sensors, precision surfaces and bearing seats several characteristic dimensions away from load points, bolts and clamps, so local deformations do not disturb them.
  • Example 1 — tensile test specimen / load cell: the gauge length (where strain is measured) is long and placed well away from the grips, so the strain gauges read the uniform stress P/AP/AP/A and not the disturbed stress near the clamps.
  • Example 2 — bolted joints: the clamping pressure of a bolt spreads only over a cone of about one plate thickness around the bolt, so bolts must be spaced closely enough (a few plate thicknesses) for the joint to be uniformly clamped and stiff.

(ii) Avoiding bending stress. A member in bending is stressed unevenly: σ=My/I\sigma=My/Iσ=My/I is maximum at the outer fibres and zero at the neutral axis, so most of the material works little and deflections are large. A member loaded axially carries σ=F/A\sigma=F/Aσ=F/A uniformly over the whole section and is much stiffer. The principle is therefore: arrange the load path so members carry tension or compression, not bending (triangulate, put loads in line with supports, avoid overhangs and eccentric loads).

Example: a 20 mm × 20 mm steel bar, 200 mm long, E=200E=200E=200 GPa, carrying 1 kN.

  • Axially: k=EAL=200×109×4×10−40.2=4×108 N/mk=\frac{EA}{L}=\frac{200\times10^9\times4\times10^{-4}}{0.2}=4\times10^8\ \text{N/m}k=LEA​=0.2200×109×4×10−4​=4×108 N/m σ=10004×10−4=2.5 MPa\sigma=\frac{1000}{4\times10^{-4}}=2.5\ \text{MPa}σ=4×10−41000​=2.5 MPa
  • As a cantilever with the load at the tip (I=b4/12I=b^4/12I=b4/12): k=3EIL3=1×106 N/m,σ=6FLb3=150 MPa.k=\frac{3EI}{L^3}=1\times10^6\ \text{N/m},\qquad \sigma=\frac{6FL}{b^3}=150\ \text{MPa}.k=L33EI​=1×106 N/m,σ=b36FL​=150 MPa.

The same bar is 400 times stiffer and has 60 times less stress when loaded axially. That is why a shelf bracket with a diagonal strut (Figure 4.1b), a bicycle frame, a crane jib or a machine frame built from triangles is far lighter than a bending-loaded design of the same stiffness.

4.7 Past Question: Classification of Loads

2024 · Q2(a)Classify the different loads to which a mechanical system is subjected. Why does it matter in design? 10Topic: load conditions
BasisType of loadDescription and example
Variation with timeStatic (steady)Constant or slowly applied: machine self-weight, preload of a bolt
Impact / shockSuddenly applied, short duration, high peak: robot hitting an end stop, punch press
Fluctuating / cyclic (fatigue)Repeated or reversed many times: rotating shaft in bending, gear teeth, crank
Random / vibrationIrregular, statistical: vehicle on a rough road, machine vibration
Type of stress producedTension / compressionAxial load: tie rod, column, piston rod (σ=F/A\sigma=F/Aσ=F/A)
ShearPins, keys, rivets (τ=F/A\tau=F/Aτ=F/A)
BendingBeams, shafts carrying gears (σ=My/I\sigma=My/Iσ=My/I)
TorsionDrive shafts (τ=Tr/J\tau=Tr/Jτ=Tr/J)
Combined / contactShaft with bending + torsion; gear-tooth and bearing contact (Hertz) stresses
DistributionConcentrated (point)Bearing reaction, gear force
Distributed / body forceSelf-weight, pressure, inertia and centrifugal forces
OriginDead, working (live), inertia, thermal, friction, environmentalWeight; payload and process forces; F=maF=maF=ma during acceleration; restrained thermal expansion; friction in guides; wind, seismic

Why it matters in design:

  1. Failure mode and criterion. Static loads are checked against yield/ultimate strength; cyclic loads against the endurance (fatigue) limit, which is much lower; impact loads against toughness and dynamic stress (a suddenly applied load gives up to twice the static stress); compressive members against buckling; contact loads against surface fatigue and wear.
  2. Correct stress formula and dimensions. The load type decides which stress equations, deflection equations and combined-stress theories apply, and therefore the section size.
  3. Factor of safety and service factor. Uncertain, impact or fluctuating loads need larger factors (application factors afa_faf​ for bearings, service factors for gears).
  4. Material and process selection: ductile and tough materials for shock, fatigue-resistant materials and good surface finish for cyclic loads.
  5. Stiffness, vibration and accuracy: dynamic loads excite resonances; the structure's natural frequency must be well above the excitation and control bandwidth.
  6. Mechatronic sizing: inertia and process loads decide actuator torque, bearing life, gear size and the disturbance the controller must reject.
  7. Cost and weight: knowing the real load avoids both failure and over-design.

4.9 Past Question: Principles of Control–Display Integration

2024 · Q4(b)List some general principles for control-display integration, taking into account human factors and ergonomics. 07Topic: ergonomics — controls and displays
  1. Spatial compatibility (proximity): place each control next to, or in the same spatial arrangement as, the display it affects (e.g. a stove's knobs laid out like its burners).
  2. Movement compatibility (population stereotypes): the display should move in the direction the user expects from the control movement: clockwise, up, right or forward = increase / "on"; a knob turned clockwise moves a pointer clockwise or a scale up.
  3. Conceptual compatibility and coding: use meanings people already hold: red = stop/danger, green = go/safe, amber = caution; standard symbols. Code controls by shape, size, colour, texture, label and location so they can be identified without looking.
  4. Grouping and arrangement: arrange controls and displays by function, sequence of use, importance and frequency of use; put the most important and most used ones in the primary zone (normal line of sight, about 15° below horizontal; within easy reach).
  5. Control–display (C/D) ratio: choose the ratio of control movement to display movement to balance fast gross positioning (low C/D) against fine adjustment (high C/D).
  6. Feedback: every control action should produce an immediate visible, audible or tactile response (detents, indicator lamps), with minimal delay.
  7. Consistency and standardization: the same control and display layout, direction and colour conventions across all panels and machines of a plant.
  8. Prevention of accidental activation and error tolerance: guards, recessed or covered switches, interlocks, two-hand controls, confirmation of critical actions; an emergency stop that is large, red, mushroom-headed and easy to reach.
  9. Anthropometry and visibility: controls within the reach envelope of the 5th–95th percentile user, displays legible (size, contrast, lighting, glare-free) and read to the precision actually needed; avoid clutter to keep the mental workload low.

5. Motion Transmission and Motor Sizing ★★★

5.1 Why Motion-Transmission Mechanisms Are Needed

Actuators produce purely rotary motion (an electric motor) or purely linear motion (a hydraulic or pneumatic cylinder). It is usually not practical to place the actuator exactly where the tool needs its motion, so a motion-transmission mechanism is placed between the actuator and the tool.

Two roles of a motion-transmission mechanism
1. It transmits motion from the actuator to the tool when the actuator cannot be placed at the tool's location with the desired type of motion (e.g. it converts rotation to translation).
2. It increases or reduces torque and speed between input and output shafts while conserving power: output power = input power − losses.

Three major categories:

  1. Rotary → rotary: gears, belts and pulleys (also chains).
  2. Rotary → translational: lead screw, ball screw, rack and pinion, belt and pulley (timing belt carrying a carriage).
  3. Cyclic motion: linkages (four-bar, slider-crank) and cams.

5.2 Mechanical Advantage, Gear Ratio and Efficiency

Mechanical advantage is the ratio of output force to input force. By energy conservation (no losses) Fidi=FodoF_id_i=F_od_oFi​di​=Fo​do​, so the ideal mechanical advantage is IMA=Fo/Fi=di/do\text{IMA}=F_o/F_i=d_i/d_oIMA=Fo​/Fi​=di​/do​: force is gained exactly as displacement is lost. For a gear pair MA=ToutTin=ωinωout=NoutNin\text{MA}=\dfrac{T_{out}}{T_{in}}=\dfrac{\omega_{in}}{\omega_{out}}=\dfrac{N_{out}}{N_{in}}MA=Tin​Tout​​=ωout​ωin​​=Nin​Nout​​.

Gear ratio, efficiency, torque and inertia reflection
Effective gear ratio (set by geometry, independent of efficiency):  N=ΔθinΔθout=ωinωout=N2N1\ N=\dfrac{\Delta\theta_{in}}{\Delta\theta_{out}}=\dfrac{\omega_{in}}{\omega_{out}}=\dfrac{N_2}{N_1} N=Δθout​Δθin​​=ωout​ωin​​=N1​N2​​
Efficiency:  η=PoutPin\ \eta=\dfrac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} η=Pin​Pout​​ (75–95 % for common mechanisms), P=TωP=T\omegaP=Tω
Output torque:  Tout=η N Tin\ T_{out}=\eta\,N\,T_{in} Tout​=ηNTin​
Load torque reflected to the input:  Tin,eff=1NηTout\ T_{in,eff}=\dfrac{1}{N\eta}T_{out} Tin,eff​=Nη1​Tout​
Load inertia reflected to the input:  Jin,eff=1N2ηJout\ J_{in,eff}=\dfrac{1}{N^2\eta}J_{out} Jin,eff​=N2η1​Jout​
Belt and pulley (no slip): x=Δθ1r1=Δθ2r2x=\Delta\theta_1r_1=\Delta\theta_2r_2x=Δθ1​r1​=Δθ2​r2​, so N=Δθ1Δθ2=r2r1=d2d1N=\dfrac{\Delta\theta_1}{\Delta\theta_2}=\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}=\dfrac{d_2}{d_1}N=Δθ2​Δθ1​​=r1​r2​​=d1​d2​​; inertia and torque reflect exactly as for gears.
Solid cylinder:  m=ρπr2l\ m=\rho\pi r^2l m=ρπr2l,  J=12mr2=12ρπl r4\ J=\tfrac12mr^2=\tfrac12\rho\pi l\,r^4 J=21​mr2=21​ρπlr4

Derivation of the reflected torque. Power balance: Toutωout=ηTinωinT_{out}\omega_{out}=\eta T_{in}\omega_{in}Tout​ωout​=ηTin​ωin​ with ωin=Nωout\omega_{in}=N\omega_{out}ωin​=Nωout​ gives Tout=ηNTinT_{out}=\eta NT_{in}Tout​=ηNTin​. The torque the motor must supply to hold a load torque ToutT_{out}Tout​ is therefore Tin,eff=Tout/(Nη)T_{in,eff}=T_{out}/(N\eta)Tin,eff​=Tout​/(Nη).

Derivation of the reflected inertia. The kinetic energy delivered to the load is η\etaη times that supplied: 12Joutθ˙out2=η⋅12Jin,effθ˙in2\tfrac12J_{out}\dot\theta_{out}^2=\eta\cdot\tfrac12J_{in,eff}\dot\theta_{in}^221​Jout​θ˙out2​=η⋅21​Jin,eff​θ˙in2​. With θ˙in=Nθ˙out\dot\theta_{in}=N\dot\theta_{out}θ˙in​=Nθ˙out​: Jout=ηJin,effN2J_{out}=\eta J_{in,eff}N^2Jout​=ηJin,eff​N2, so Jin,eff=Jout/(N2η)J_{in,eff}=J_{out}/(N^2\eta)Jin,eff​=Jout​/(N2η). A large reduction ratio makes a heavy load look very light to the motor.

Rotary-to-linear mechanisms (for reference). Lead/ball screw of lead ppp (m/rev): x=p θ/2πx=p\,\theta/2\pix=pθ/2π; a translating mass mmm reflects as Jeff=m(p/2π)2/ηJ_{eff}=m(p/2\pi)^2/\etaJeff​=m(p/2π)2/η and a force FFF as T=Fp/(2πη)T=Fp/(2\pi\eta)T=Fp/(2πη). A lead screw has sliding contact (low efficiency, often self-locking, cheap); a ball screw has recirculating balls (rolling contact, 90 %+ efficiency, precise, back-drivable, more expensive). Rack and pinion or belt of pulley radius rrr: x=rθx=r\thetax=rθ, Jeff=mr2J_{eff}=mr^2Jeff​=mr2.

5.3 Inertia Matching Between Motor and Load

A rule of thumb is that the ratio of motor inertia to reflected load inertia should lie between 1:1 and 1:10; the 1:1 match is optimal for a purely inertial load.

Proof. A motor (rotor inertia JmJ_mJm​) drives a purely inertial load JlJ_lJl​ through ratio NNN (θ¨m=Nθ¨l\ddot\theta_m=N\ddot\theta_lθ¨m​=Nθ¨l​): Tm=(Jm+1N2Jl)θ¨m=(Jm+1N2Jl)Nθ¨l.T_m=\Big(J_m+\frac{1}{N^2}J_l\Big)\ddot\theta_m=\Big(J_m+\frac{1}{N^2}J_l\Big)N\ddot\theta_l.Tm​=(Jm​+N21​Jl​)θ¨m​=(Jm​+N21​Jl​)Nθ¨l​. Heating is Pelec=Ri2P_{elec}=Ri^2Pelec​=Ri2 and Tm∝iT_m\propto iTm​∝i, so minimum heating = minimum TmT_mTm​. For a required load acceleration θ¨l\ddot\theta_lθ¨l​: dTmdN=(Jm+JlN2)θ¨l+(−2NN4Jl)Nθ¨l=θ¨l(Jm−JlN2)=0\frac{dT_m}{dN}=\Big(J_m+\frac{J_l}{N^2}\Big)\ddot\theta_l+\Big(-\frac{2N}{N^4}J_l\Big)N\ddot\theta_l=\ddot\theta_l\Big(J_m-\frac{J_l}{N^2}\Big)=0dNdTm​​=(Jm​+N2Jl​​)θ¨l​+(−N42N​Jl​)Nθ¨l​=θ¨l​(Jm​−N2Jl​​)=0 ⇒ Jm=1N2Jl=Jl,reflected,Nopt=Jl/Jm.\Rightarrow\ J_m=\frac{1}{N^2}J_l=J_{l,\text{reflected}},\qquad N_{opt}=\sqrt{J_l/J_m}.⇒ Jm​=N21​Jl​=Jl,reflected​,Nopt​=Jl​/Jm​​.

CAUTIONThe 1:1 match is optimal only for purely inertial loads. If friction or process loads dominate, the ideal inertia match may not be a good design.

5.4 Motion Profiles and Motor Sizing Procedure

A point-to-point axis moves a distance Δθ\Delta\thetaΔθ in a cycle tcyct_{cyc}tcyc​ with a trapezoidal speed profile (acceleration tat_ata​, constant speed trt_rtr​, deceleration tdt_dtd​, dwell tdwt_{dw}tdw​) or, when tr=0t_r=0tr​=0, a triangular one. The distance is the area under the speed–time curve.

Motor sizing formulas (direct drive, no gear)
Trapezoid:  Δθ=θ˙r(ta2+tr+td2)\ \Delta\theta=\dot\theta_r\Big(\dfrac{t_a}{2}+t_r+\dfrac{t_d}{2}\Big) Δθ=θ˙r​(2ta​​+tr​+2td​​); triangle:  Δθ=θ˙r ta+td2\ \Delta\theta=\dot\theta_r\,\dfrac{t_a+t_d}{2} Δθ=θ˙r​2ta​+td​​
Accelerations:  θ¨a=θ˙r/ta\ \ddot\theta_a=\dot\theta_r/t_a θ¨a​=θ˙r​/ta​,  θ¨d=−θ˙r/td\ \ddot\theta_d=-\dot\theta_r/t_d θ¨d​=−θ˙r​/td​,  θ¨r=θ¨dw=0\ \ddot\theta_r=\ddot\theta_{dw}=0 θ¨r​=θ¨dw​=0
Torque in each segment:  T=(Jm+Jl)θ¨+Tload\ T=(J_m+J_l)\ddot\theta+T_{load} T=(Jm​+Jl​)θ¨+Tload​
Peak torque:  Tmax=max⁡∣Ti∣\ T_{max}=\max|T_i| Tmax​=max∣Ti​∣; RMS (continuous) torque: Trms=[1tcyc(Ta2ta+Tr2tr+Td2td+Tdw2tdw)]1/2T_{rms}=\left[\frac{1}{t_{cyc}}\big(T_a^2t_a+T_r^2t_r+T_d^2t_d+T_{dw}^2t_{dw}\big)\right]^{1/2}Trms​=[tcyc​1​(Ta2​ta​+Tr2​tr​+Td2​td​+Tdw2​tdw​)]1/2 Motor specification: rotor inertia (≈ JlJ_lJl​ for a 1:1 match), maximum speed ≥θ˙r\ge\dot\theta_r≥θ˙r​, peak torque ≥Tmax\ge T_{max}≥Tmax​, continuous (RMS) torque ≥Trms\ge T_{rms}≥Trms​, with a safety margin; peak power Tmaxθ˙rT_{max}\dot\theta_rTmax​θ˙r​.

Lecture example (imperial): steel disc d=3d=3d=3 in, l=2l=2l=2 in, ρ=0.286\rho=0.286ρ=0.286 lb/in³, ¼ rev in 250 ms with ta=tr=td=50t_a=t_r=t_d=50ta​=tr​=td​=50 ms, tdw=100t_{dw}=100tdw​=100 ms. Jl=120.286386π(2)(1.5)4=0.0118J_l=\tfrac12\frac{0.286}{386}\pi(2)(1.5)^4=0.0118Jl​=21​3860.286​π(2)(1.5)4=0.0118 lb·in·s², Jm=JlJ_m=J_lJm​=Jl​, θ˙r=150\dot\theta_r=150θ˙r​=150 rev/min, θ¨=100π\ddot\theta=100\piθ¨=100π rad/s², Ta=0.0236(100π)=7.414T_a=0.0236(100\pi)=7.414Ta​=0.0236(100π)=7.414 lb·in, Trms=4.689T_{rms}=4.689Trms​=4.689 lb·in → choose a motor with rotor inertia ≈ 0.0118 lb·in·s², ≥ 150 rev/min, peak/RMS torque ratings about 8.0 and 5.0 lb·in. Practical consideration: servo motors deliver their power at 1500–5000 rev/min, so a 10:1–20:1 gear reducer between motor and load is worth considering, followed by repeating the sizing.

5.5 Past Question: Roles and Types of Motion Transmission

2022 · Q3(b)What are the roles of motion transmission in mechatronic system? What are the three major types of motion transmission? 07Topic: motion transmission — roles and types

Actuators give purely rotary or purely linear motion and usually cannot be placed where the tool needs its motion, so a transmission mechanism is placed between them. Its roles are:

  1. To transmit motion from the actuator to the tool when the actuator cannot be designed into the same location as the tool, or does not have the desired type of motion (e.g. converting a motor's rotation into the straight-line motion of a table).
  2. To change torque and speed (increase or reduce them) between the input and output shafts while conserving power, Pout=Pin−lossesP_{out}=P_{in}-\text{losses}Pout​=Pin​−losses, i.e. Tout=ηNTinT_{out}=\eta NT_{in}Tout​=ηNTin​ and ωout=ωin/N\omega_{out}=\omega_{in}/Nωout​=ωin​/N. This lets a small, fast motor drive a slow, heavy load and changes the load inertia seen by the motor (J/N2J/N^2J/N2).

Three major types (Figure 5.1): (1) rotary-to-rotary (gears, belts and pulleys); (2) rotary-to-translational (lead screw, ball screw, rack and pinion, belt and pulley); (3) cyclic motion (linkages and cams).

Source lectureAJ · L5 – Motion Transmission (5. Motion Transmission.pdf, pp. 3–5)

6. Controller Design and Tuning ★★★

6.1 Control Laws and Their Effects

A controller compares the measured output yyy with the set point rrr and computes the actuator command uuu from the error e=r−ye=r-ye=r−y. The common control laws are:

On–offu=umaxu=u_{max}u=umax​ if e>0e>0e>0, uminu_{min}umin​ if e<0e<0e<0 (with hysteresis)Simple and cheap; output cycles around the set point (thermostats)

Other control laws: cascade, feedforward, ratio, model predictive (MPC), state feedback, fuzzy and adaptive control.

6.3 Lag Compensator Design by the Root Locus

A lag compensator is used when the transient response is already acceptable but the steady-state error is too large. The design keeps the closed-loop dominant poles where they are and raises the static error constant.

  1. From the overshoot specification find ζ=−ln⁡(%OS/100)π2+ln⁡2(%OS/100)\zeta=\dfrac{-\ln(\%OS/100)}{\sqrt{\pi^2+\ln^2(\%OS/100)}}ζ=π2+ln2(%OS/100)​−ln(%OS/100)​ (choose a slightly larger ζ\zetaζ as a margin).
  2. On the uncompensated root locus find the gain KKK that places the poles on that ζ\zetaζ line; compute the uncompensated error constant (e.g. KvK_vKv​).
  3. Required improvement factor =Kv,req/Kv,unc=zc/pc=K_{v,req}/K_{v,unc}=z_c/p_c=Kv,req​/Kv,unc​=zc​/pc​.
  4. Choose zcz_czc​ small compared with the real part of the dominant poles (about 1/10–1/20 of it) and pc=zc/(factor)p_c=z_c/(\text{factor})pc​=zc​/(factor); the pole–zero "dipole" near the origin hardly moves the dominant poles.
  5. Check by simulation: the dipole adds a slow closed-loop pole near −zc-z_c−zc​ with a small residue, which slightly raises the overshoot and leaves a slow tail.

Static error constants and steady-state errors (unity feedback):

6.4 Controller Tuning: Ziegler–Nichols Methods

Controller tuning is the adjustment of the controller parameters (for a PID: KcK_cKc​, τI\tau_IτI​, τD\tau_DτD​) so that the closed loop meets its performance specifications: stability with a margin, speed of response, small overshoot, zero offset, good disturbance rejection and robustness to model error. Methods include trial and error, Ziegler–Nichols (open-loop step and closed-loop continuous cycling), Cohen–Coon, direct synthesis and internal model control (IMC), integral-error criteria (IAE, ITAE) and relay auto-tuning.

KKK = process gain Δy/Δu\Delta y/\Delta uΔy/Δu, LLL = dead time, TTT = time constant (from the reaction curve); KuK_uKu​ = ultimate gain and PuP_uPu​ = ultimate period of sustained oscillation. Both sets aim at a quarter-decay ratio response.

6.5 Internal Model Control (IMC)

In IMC the controller contains a model G~p\tilde G_pG~p​ of the process, run in parallel with it. The difference d~=y−G~pu\tilde d=y-\tilde G_pud~=y−G~p​u carries the effect of disturbances and model error and is fed back. If the model were perfect and Q=G~p−1Q=\tilde G_p^{-1}Q=G~p−1​, the output would follow the set point exactly. Because a dead time or a right-half-plane zero cannot be inverted, the model is factored as G~p=G~+G~−\tilde G_p=\tilde G_+\tilde G_-G~p​=G~+​G~−​ (G~+\tilde G_+G~+​: non-invertible part with steady-state gain 1) and only G~−\tilde G_-G~−​ is inverted, with a low-pass filter f=1/(τcs+1)rf=1/(\tau_cs+1)^rf=1/(τc​s+1)r for physical realisability and robustness. The equivalent classical feedback controller is Gc=Q1−G~pQG_c=\dfrac{Q}{1-\tilde G_pQ}Gc​=1−G~p​QQ​. The single tuning parameter τc\tau_cτc​ (closed-loop time constant) trades speed against robustness.

6.6 Past Question: Phase-Lead and Phase-Lag Compensation

2022 · Q4(a)Write short notes on the following terms. (i) Phase lead compensation (ii) Phase lag compensation 08Topic: lead and lag compensators

(i) Phase-lead compensation. A lead compensator Gc(s)=Kcs+zcs+pcG_c(s)=K_c\dfrac{s+z_c}{s+p_c}Gc​(s)=Kc​s+pc​s+zc​​ with zc<pcz_c<p_czc​<pc​ (equivalently KcαTs+1αTs+1K_c\alpha\dfrac{Ts+1}{\alpha Ts+1}Kc​ααTs+1Ts+1​, α<1\alpha<1α<1) adds positive phase (up to ϕm\phi_mϕm​, where sin⁡ϕm=1−α1+α\sin\phi_m=\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}sinϕm​=1+α1−α​, at ωm=zcpc\omega_m=\sqrt{z_cp_c}ωm​=zc​pc​​) and raises the high-frequency gain (Figure 6.1, left).

  • Used to improve the transient response and stability: increases the phase margin and damping, reduces overshoot, increases bandwidth and speed (shorter rise and settling times).
  • In the root locus it pulls the locus to the left, so the dominant poles can be placed at a faster, better-damped location.
  • It behaves like an approximate PD controller; it has little effect on steady-state error, and the higher high-frequency gain amplifies sensor noise.

(ii) Phase-lag compensation. A lag compensator with zc>pcz_c>p_czc​>pc​, both placed close to the origin (KcβTs+1βTs+1K_c\beta\dfrac{Ts+1}{\beta Ts+1}Kc​ββTs+1Ts+1​, β>1\beta>1β>1), gives a low-frequency gain increase of β=zc/pc\beta=z_c/p_cβ=zc​/pc​ while adding only a small phase lag near crossover (Figure 6.1, right).

  • Used to improve the steady-state accuracy: multiplies KpK_pKp​, KvK_vKv​ or KaK_aKa​ by β\betaβ and so divides the steady-state error by β\betaβ, while the transient response (dominant poles) stays nearly unchanged.
  • It attenuates high frequencies (good noise rejection) but lowers the bandwidth a little and adds a slow closed-loop pole that gives a slow "tail" in the response.
  • It behaves like an approximate PI controller.

A lead–lag compensator combines both: lead for transient response, lag for steady-state accuracy.
