6.8 Past Question: Controller Tuning and the Open-Loop Ziegler–Nichols Method

2022 · Q4(c)What is controller tuning? Briefly describe the procedure of open-loop Ziegler-Nichols (Z-N) PID tuning method. 12Topic: Z–N open-loop tuning

Controller tuning is the process of selecting and adjusting the parameters of a controller (for a PID: the proportional gain KpK_pKp​, integral time TiT_iTi​ and derivative time TdT_dTd​) so that the closed-loop system meets the performance requirements: stable with adequate margins, fast, with acceptable overshoot, no offset and good disturbance rejection, and robust to changes in the process.

Open-loop (process reaction curve / step) Z–N procedure:

  1. Bring the process to steady state with the controller in manual (loop open).
  2. Apply a small step change Δu\Delta uΔu to the controller output (the manipulated variable, e.g. valve opening or motor voltage).
  3. Record the process output y(t)y(t)y(t) until it settles: the process reaction curve, an S-shaped curve for a self-regulating process (Figure 6.2).
  4. Draw the tangent at the inflection point (point of maximum slope). Its intersection with the initial level gives the dead time LLL; its intersection with the final level gives L+TL+TL+T, so the time constant TTT follows. The process gain is K=Δy/ΔuK=\Delta y/\Delta uK=Δy/Δu (the slope of the tangent is R=K/TR=K/TR=K/T per unit step). This fits the model Ke−Ls/(Ts+1)Ke^{-Ls}/(Ts+1)Ke−Ls/(Ts+1).
  5. Calculate the settings from the Z–N table: P: Kp=TKLK_p=\dfrac{T}{KL}Kp​=KLT​; PI: Kp=0.9TKLK_p=0.9\dfrac{T}{KL}Kp​=0.9KLT​, Ti=3.33LT_i=3.33LTi​=3.33L; PID: Kp=1.2TKLK_p=1.2\dfrac{T}{KL}Kp​=1.2KLT​, Ti=2LT_i=2LTi​=2L, Td=0.5LT_d=0.5LTd​=0.5L.
  6. Put the controller in automatic with these settings and fine-tune on line (the Z–N settings aim at quarter-decay, which is fairly oscillatory; KpK_pKp​ is often reduced).

Conditions: the process must be open-loop stable and self-regulating (S-shaped curve, no integrator, no oscillation); the method works best for 0.1<L/T<10.1\lt L/T\lt10.1<L/T<1; the test should be done when disturbances are small, because noise makes the tangent inaccurate.

6.9 Past Question: Controller Tuning, Purpose and Common Control Laws

2023 · Q4(a)What is controller tuning? What are the purposes of using a controller? Name some of the controllers (control law) usually used. 10Topic: controller tuning and control laws

Controller tuning is the selection and adjustment of controller parameters (e.g. KcK_cKc​, τI\tau_IτI​, τD\tau_DτD​ of a PID) so that the closed loop has the desired behaviour: stability with margins, fast response, small overshoot, zero offset, good disturbance rejection and robustness. Methods: trial and error, Ziegler–Nichols (step and continuous cycling), Cohen–Coon, IMC/direct synthesis, ITAE and auto-tuning.

Purposes of using a controller:

  1. Keep the controlled variable at its set point despite disturbances (regulation), e.g. temperature of an oven when the door opens.
  2. Make the output follow a changing set point (servo/tracking), e.g. a robot joint following a trajectory.
  3. Stabilise an unstable process (magnetic levitation, inverted pendulum) and improve damping.
  4. Improve speed of response and accuracy (remove steady-state error) beyond what the open-loop process gives.
  5. Reduce sensitivity to parameter changes and model errors; ensure safety, product quality and efficient use of energy and material.

Controllers (control laws) usually used: on–off (two-position) control; proportional (P); proportional-integral (PI); proportional-derivative (PD); proportional-integral-derivative (PID), with variants such as PI-D and I-PD (derivative or proportional action on the measurement only); lead, lag and lead–lag compensators; cascade, feedforward and ratio control; state feedback; model predictive control (MPC); adaptive and fuzzy-logic control.

Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §6.1 and §6.4 of this book)

6.10 Past Question: Why the Z–N Step Method Is Preferred to Continuous Cycling

2023 · Q4(b)Why Z-N step method for tuning is better than Z-N continuous cycling method? 10Topic: Z–N step vs continuous cycling

Continuous cycling (closed-loop) method: with I and D actions off, the proportional gain is raised step by step until the loop oscillates with constant amplitude; the ultimate gain KuK_uKu​ and period PuP_uPu​ are recorded and used in the table of §6.4. Step (open-loop) method: a single step is applied with the loop open, and KKK, LLL, TTT are read from the reaction curve (§6.8).

The step method is better because:

PointZ–N step (open-loop) methodZ–N continuous cycling (closed-loop) method
SafetyThe process is never taken to the stability limit; only a small, controlled step upsetThe loop must be driven to the edge of instability; a little too much gain gives growing oscillations, which can damage equipment or be unsafe
Time and production lossOne test, finished when the response settlesMany trial-and-error gain increases, each waiting for the response; long test with the process oscillating, product off-specification
ApplicabilityWorks for any open-loop stable, self-regulating processImpossible for processes that never oscillate under P control (first- or second-order without dead time); not allowed in many plants
Information obtainedA process model Ke−Ls/(Ts+1)Ke^{-Ls}/(Ts+1)Ke−Ls/(Ts+1), usable for other rules (Cohen–Coon, IMC, ITAE) and for simulationOnly two numbers (KuK_uKu​, PuP_uPu​) at one frequency
Disturbance of the plantProcess upset is one-off and bounded by the step sizeSustained oscillation disturbs connected units and wears actuators

Limitations of the step method (for a balanced answer): it needs an open-loop stable process; the tangent construction is sensitive to measurement noise and to disturbances during the test; and the process must be allowed to run in manual. Even so, because it is quicker, safer and gives a model, the step method is usually preferred.

7. Optimization of Mechatronic Systems ★★★

7.1 What Optimization Is

Definition
Optimization is the act of obtaining the best result under given circumstances: finding the values of the design variables that minimise (or maximise) an objective such as cost, weight, energy or error, while satisfying all constraints. In mechatronics it is mainly used to establish the optimal system configuration, and also to find optimal trajectories, to design control systems and to identify model parameters.

Examples from other fields: minimising the weight of aircraft components; operating a process plant at its optimal production rate; designing mechanical components for minimum manufacturing cost or maximum life.

Statement of an optimization (mathematical programming) problem
Find  X={x1x2⋮xn}  which minimizes  f(X)\text{Find }\ \mathbf X=\begin{Bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\ \vdots\\x_n\end{Bmatrix}\ \text{ which minimizes }\ f(\mathbf X)Find  X=⎩⎨⎧​x1​x2​⋮xn​​⎭⎬⎫​  which minimizes  f(X) subject togj(X)≤0,  j=1,…,m;lj(X)=0,  j=1,…,p.\text{subject to}\quad g_j(\mathbf X)\le0,\ \ j=1,\dots,m;\qquad l_j(\mathbf X)=0,\ \ j=1,\dots,p.subject togj​(X)≤0,  j=1,…,m;lj​(X)=0,  j=1,…,p. X\mathbf XX = design vector, fff = objective function, gjg_jgj​ = inequality constraints, ljl_jlj​ = equality constraints. Without constraints the problem is unconstrained. Maximising fff is the same as minimising −f-f−f.

7.2 Formulating an Optimal-Design Problem

The formulation follows a hierarchy (lecture flowchart): need for optimization → choose design variables → formulate constraints → formulate objective function → set variable bounds → choose an optimization algorithm → obtain solution(s), with feedback to earlier steps when needed.

  1. Design variables: the parameters that are highly sensitive to proper functioning and are varied during the optimization; others stay fixed. Thumb rule 1: choose as few design variables as possible (speed and efficiency of the algorithm depend on their number).
  2. Constraints: functional relationships representing physical phenomena and resource limits. Inequality constraints (most common, e.g. stress σ(x)≤Sallow\sigma(x)\le S_{allow}σ(x)≤Sallow​, natural frequency ν(x)≥2\nu(x)\ge2ν(x)≥2 Hz; one type converts to the other by multiplying by −1) and equality constraints (e.g. deflection δ(x)=5\delta(x)=5δ(x)=5 mm), which are harder and can be relaxed into two inequalities (4≤δ≤64\le\delta\le64≤δ≤6). Thumb rule 2: keep the number of complex equality constraints as low as possible.
  3. Objective function: minimise undesirable things (cost, weight) or maximise desirable ones (profit, life). Normally a single objective is chosen and the other objectives become constraints (e.g. minimise truss weight subject to a deflection limit).
  4. Variable bounds: xi(L)≤xi≤xi(U)x_i^{(L)}\le x_i\le x_i^{(U)}xi(L)​≤xi​≤xi(U)​. If the optimum lands on a bound, the bound may be wrong and should be re-examined.

Classes of algorithms: single-variable (direct and gradient-based); multivariable (direct and gradient-based); constrained (use the previous ones while staying inside the feasible region); specialised (integer programming, geometric programming); non-traditional (genetic algorithms, simulated annealing).

7.3 Optimality Criteria (Single Variable)

  • Local minimum x∗x^*x∗: f(x∗)≤f(x∗+h)f(x^*)\le f(x^*+h)f(x∗)≤f(x∗+h) for all sufficiently small positive and negative hhh (no better point in the neighbourhood).
  • Global minimum: no point in the entire search space has a smaller value.
  • Inflection point: the function increases on one side and decreases on the other (e.g. x=0x=0x=0 for f=x3f=x^3f=x3).
Derivative test
At a stationary point (f′(x∗)=0f'(x^*)=0f′(x∗)=0) let nnn be the order of the first non-zero higher derivative: if nnn is odd, x∗x^*x∗ is an inflection point; if nnn is even, it is a local optimum — a minimum if that derivative is positive, a maximum if negative.

Lecture example 1. f(x)=x2+54/xf(x)=x^2+54/xf(x)=x2+54/x: f′=2x−54/x2=0⇒x∗=3f'=2x-54/x^2=0\Rightarrow x^*=3f′=2x−54/x2=0⇒x∗=3; f′′=2+108/x3=6>0f''=2+108/x^3=6>0f′′=2+108/x3=6>0 at x=3x=3x=3 (n=2n=2n=2, even, positive) → local minimum, f(3)=27f(3)=27f(3)=27.

7.4 Past Question: Optimization of a System

2022 · Q1(d)What is meant by optimization of a system? 04Topic: definition of optimization

Optimization of a system means obtaining the best result under the given circumstances: choosing the values of the design variables of the system (dimensions, gear ratio, controller gains, motor size …) that minimise or maximise an objective function (e.g. minimise cost, weight, energy or tracking error; maximise efficiency or life) while satisfying all constraints (stress, deflection, speed, power limits, variable bounds). Mathematically: find X\mathbf XX that minimises f(X)f(\mathbf X)f(X) subject to gj(X)≤0g_j(\mathbf X)\le0gj​(X)≤0 and lj(X)=0l_j(\mathbf X)=0lj​(X)=0.

In mechatronics it is used to establish the optimal system configuration, to identify optimal trajectories, to design the control system and to identify model parameters. Example: choosing the gear ratio that minimises motor heating (Nopt=Jl/JmN_{opt}=\sqrt{J_l/J_m}Nopt​=Jl​/Jm​​, §5.3).

Source lectureAJ · Opt – Optimization (Optimization.pdf, p. 1)
